title: Maronea silver strike and the building of the Themistoclean fleet
summary: In 483/2 BCE, during the archonship of Nicomedes, a rich vein of silver was struck at Maronea in the Laurion mining district of Attica, yielding a hundred talents for the Athenian treasury. Instead of a per-capita dividend, Themistocles persuaded the assembly to fund the construction of one hundred triremes. This expanded fleet defeated the Persian navy at Salamis in 480 BCE, securing Athenian maritime supremacy.

uncertainty.note: Discovery of the Maronea ore and assembly vote occurred in the Athenian archon year of Nicomedes (483/2 BCE); the newly built fleet fought at Salamis in 480 BCE.

as_recorded.calendar: BCE (Aristotle, Ath. Pol. 22.7, trans. Sir Frederic G. Kenyon)
as_recorded.value: Two years later, in the archonship of Nicodemus, the mines of Maroneia were discovered, and the state made a profit of a hundred talents from the working of them

as_recorded.calendar: BCE (Danielle L. Kellogg, review of Ben Akrigg, sehepunkte 21, 2021)
as_recorded.value: determines that more than 30,000 male slaves were needed for service in the silver mines and in the Athenian navy

where.historical_name: Maroneia, Laurion mining district, Attica, polis of Athens

importance.justification: The Maronea strike and Themistocles' naval bill transformed Athens into a major maritime power and provided the fleet that defeated Xerxes' invasion at Salamis.

audience_note: Documents perilous subterranean chattel slavery in the Laurion silver extraction galleries.

related.because: The 100 triremes financed by the Maronea silver strike formed the naval backbone of the Greek victory at Salamis.

reviewer_note: Least sure of whether the Athenian assembly funded 100 triremes (as in Ath. Pol. 22.7) or 200 (as reported in Herodotus 7.144), and of the manuscript reading of the archon's name (Nicomedes versus Nicodemus).
